title: A look back at #MeToo
gist: In a podcast intro on #MeToo's legacy, Yglesias sets aside the 'did it go too far' debate and asks whether the movement went anywhere at all, arguing that Catharine MacKinnon's own sexual-harassment legal infrastructure — not the movement — is what forced corporate America to build norm-propagating machinery and made a conspiracy of silence necessary to protect Harvey Weinstein. He faults #MeToo for the flaws of leaderless internet movements: no spokespeople, no definitions, and attention driven by fame and media cycles rather than harm or policy. (Paid episode; only the show-notes text is available.)

insights.claim: The interesting question about #MeToo is not whether it went too far — an overblown narrative — but whether it went anywhere at all and how its pieces fit together.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Reframes a decade-old culture-war debate around measurable institutional change instead of backlash narratives.
insights.quote: an overblown narrative, in my view

insights.claim: The movement was aimed at shifting norms rather than at formal legislative change, a reading anchored in Catharine MacKinnon's claim that '#MeToo has done what the law could not.'
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Sets the standard by which the movement should be evaluated: norm diffusion, not statute count.
insights.quote: #MeToo has done what the law could not
insights.locator: She argues that the movement was more about shifting norms

insights.claim: MacKinnon's framing undersells her own contribution, because the legal infrastructure for sexual harassment litigation is what pushed corporate America to build norm-propagating machinery, and that in turn is why protecting Harvey Weinstein required an active conspiracy of silence.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: A general model of how law changes behavior indirectly: liability exposure forces firms to build internal compliance culture.
insights.quote: Creating the legal infrastructure for sexual harassment litigation induced corporate America to create its own infrastructure

insights.claim: A central paradox of the era is that the Harvey Weinstein exposés that set the movement in motion revealed behavior everyone had already agreed was unacceptable.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: If the norms already existed, the binding constraint was enforcement and information, not consensus — a different problem with different solutions.
insights.quote: revealed behavior that everyone had already agreed wasn't acceptable
insights.locator: I think one of the paradoxes of the era

insights.claim: The labor-intensive investigative reporting required to expose Weinstein simply cannot be replicated in every workplace, making journalism a structurally non-scalable enforcement mechanism.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Any accountability regime that depends on investigative capacity will produce coverage proportional to newsworthiness, not to harm.
insights.quote: the level of labor-intensive investigation that went into exposing him simply can't be done in every workplace

insights.claim: Because #MeToo was scattershot and journalism-driven, which cases received attention tracked how famous the perpetrator was rather than the scale of his misdeeds.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Explains the selection bias in what the public treats as evidence about the movement's reach and fairness.
insights.quote: focus often seemed more a function of how famous the perpetrator was than of the scale of his misdeeds

insights.claim: These cases typically lack the incontrovertible proof that formal law enforcement requires, and many victims have good reasons not to want to be at the center of a legal proceeding — so legal remedies were never the natural channel.

themes.theme: Leaderless movements in the internet era

insights.claim: #MeToo displayed the characteristic flaws of postmodern leaderless internet-era social movements: no authoritative spokespeople, few clear definitions, and no explicit policy objectives.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: A reusable template for evaluating any viral movement's likely durability — absence of spokespeople predicts absence of durable policy output.
insights.quote: had a lot of the characteristic flaws of postmodern leaderless social movements in the internet era
insights.locator: I am hung up on the fact

insights.claim: The movement's attention crested and then waned for reasons tied to media dynamics rather than to any clear policy shift, and the question of which men have been forgiven, by whom, and in what sense remains unresolved.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Attention cycles, not institutional milestones, governed the arc — meaning the movement's apparent conclusion carries little information about outcomes.
insights.quote: Attention crested and then waned for reasons that seem to have more to do with media dynamics than with clear policy shifts.
insights.locator: I am hung up on the fact

insights.claim: The optimistic counter-case rests on broad evidence that progressive views about gender roles are becoming more entrenched, implying durable norm change even absent formal legal or policy wins.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: The empirical crux: if attitude data really is ratcheting, norm-based movements deliver returns that policy scorecards miss.
insights.quote: broad evidence that progressive views about gender roles are becoming more entrenched
